name: Alfalfa
notes:
A feed crop, not eaten by people. It's in the dataset so animal foods can charge for the alfalfa they eat (mainly dairy and lamb).

Yield (~8.5 t/ha) and water come from general agronomic sources, and its pesticide profile is insecticides (malathion, carbaryl, diazinon). Alfalfa fixes its own nitrogen, so it needs no nitrogen fertilizer, and as a perennial it is rarely tilled.

When alfalfa is fed to animals, the farm-gate emission figure is used (crop production only, ~0.35–0.4 kg CO2e/kg world, 0.15 US). Retail stages aren't charged, because feed never goes through a shop. That was added on 2026-09-24. The world emission values are not from a verified source (confidence 2); the US value is from Adom et al. 2012.

Minerals are an estimate from a livestock feed table (Feedipedia, alfalfa hay), because USDA has no record for alfalfa as it isn't a human food. Vitamins and selenium are left out.

Vitamin B12 and EPA/DHA are taken as 0 (plants don't make them).

Only alfalfa sprouts are listed. So minerals come from Feedipedia's alfalfa hay feed table (averages of many lab samples), converted from per-kg dry matter to as-fed using its average dry matter of 89.4%. Per kg dry matter: calcium 16.8 g, phosphorus 2.6 g, potassium 24.6 g, magnesium 2.3 g, zinc 27 mg, iron 587 mg (iron is a single sample and hay iron often includes soil, so it is especially rough). As-fed per gram: calcium 15.02 mg, phosphorus 2.32 mg, potassium 21.99 mg, magnesium 2.06 mg, zinc 0.024 mg, iron 0.52 mg. Vitamins and selenium are left out: Feedipedia gives no vitamin values, vitamin levels in hay drop a lot during drying and storage (vitamin C is mostly destroyed), and selenium depends on the soil, so any number would be a guess. Mineral content also varies with cutting stage and soil.

source.title: Poore & Nemecek (2018) — Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers (Science)
source.note: Alfalfa — emissions_per_kg: LCA literature places irrigated US alfalfa at 0.2–0.4 kg CO2e/kg. P&N 2018 meta-analysis of 38,700 farms covers all major animal feed crops; alfalfa's low-emission profile is driven by nitrogen-fixation (reducing synthetic N fertilizer demand), perennial root system (low tillage), and high yield diluting per-kg fixed costs. Value of 0.4 kg CO2e/kg represents the upper bound for commercially irrigated alfalfa (irrigation energy is the dominant emission source in water-intensive production regions such as California's Central Valley). CORRECTION 2026-09-24: P&N 2018 does not report alfalfa (no forage products in Supplementary Table S1), so 0.4 is not a P&N number; it comes from unspecified LCA literature. It is already a crop-production (farm-gate) figure, not cradle-to-retail. Confidence lowered 3 -> 2.

source.title: FAO — Alfalfa Crop Information
source.note: Alfalfa — emissions_per_kg: FAO crop information confirms alfalfa's low GHG footprint relative to other forage crops due to biological nitrogen fixation (BNF) reducing synthetic N2O emissions and perennial growth habit reducing tillage-related CO2. Consistent with LCA studies reporting 0.2–0.35 kg CO2e/kg for rain-fed or minimally irrigated systems; 0.35 used as a conservative midpoint for globally mixed production. CORRECTION 2026-09-24: the cited FAO crop-information URL now returns 404, and FAO's crop-information pages cover water and yield, not GHG; the 0.35 could not be verified. It is a crop-production (farm-gate) figure. Confidence lowered 3 -> 2.

name: Grass Hay
notes:
A feed crop for cattle, sheep and goats. Not eaten by people.

Yield (~5.5 t/ha), water, fertilizer and pesticide values are general agronomic estimates. Emissions are low, because it's a perennial grass with little tillage and modest fertilizer. Animal foods use the farm-gate figure (0.25–0.3 world, 0.14 US from Adom et al. 2012), so retail stages are not charged to feed.

Grass grazed directly on pasture is NOT counted here. It's counted through each animal's pasture area. Grass hay only covers hay that's cut and fed.

Minerals are an estimate from a livestock feed table (Feedipedia, timothy hay), because USDA has no record for hay as it isn't a human food. Vitamins and selenium are left out.

Vitamin B12 and EPA/DHA are taken as 0 (plants don't make them).

name: Fishmeal
notes:
Ground, dried fish (mostly Peruvian anchoveta) fed to farmed salmon, shrimp, pigs and chickens. It's not eaten by people. It's here so those animals are charged for it.

The key number is wild fish killed: about 3.6 kg of whole fish makes 1 kg of fishmeal plus fish oil. About 30% of fishmeal comes from trimmings of fish already caught for food, so 2.55 kg of fish are killed per kg of fishmeal. Each anchoveta (~18 g, ~15.6 million neurons, estimated from brain-scaling rules) counts as a direct kill for whatever animal eats the feed.

Emissions for feed use are from a 2025 Peruvian LCA: ~0.32 kg CO2e/kg, covering fishing, reduction and export. The older 6–6.5 retail-style figures are kept for reference only. Fishmeal has no land or crop water.

Minerals are an estimate from a livestock feed table (Feedipedia, fish meal 65% protein), because USDA has no record for fishmeal as it isn't a human food. Omega-3 is a guess from the fat content and sardine oil's fatty acids. Vitamins are left out.

Vitamins are a guess scaled up from raw anchovy. Drying heat destroys some of them, so real values are probably lower.

source.title: FAO (2014) — Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sectors
source.note: Fishmeal — nutrition: Feed-grade fishmeal (low-temperature/steam-dried) proximate composition per gram: protein 0.60–0.70, fat 0.08–0.12, ash 0.15–0.20, moisture ~0.10. Human nutritional database values are not applicable (feed ingredient); macros derived from standard fishmeal product specifications reported in the FAO aquaculture sector documentation.

source.title: Feedipedia — Fish meal, type 65 protein (INRAE, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO feed tables)
source.note: Fishmeal — ESTIMATE, not a human-food measurement. Checked 2026-10-02: USDA FoodData Central's SR Legacy, Foundation and Branded datasets have no record for it (searched the full downloads), because USDA only covers foods people eat. Minerals come from Feedipedia's 'Fish meal, type 65 protein' feed table (70.7% protein in dry matter = 65% as fed, matching this entry), converted to as-fed with its average dry matter of 92.1%. Per kg dry matter: calcium 44.8 g, phosphorus 28.6 g, potassium 8.5 g, magnesium 2.4 g, zinc 107 mg, iron 382 mg, selenium 0.4 mg (selenium from only 3 samples). As-fed per gram: calcium 41.26 mg, phosphorus 26.34 mg, potassium 7.83 mg, magnesium 2.21 mg, zinc 0.099 mg, iron 0.35 mg, selenium 0.37 µg. Calcium and phosphorus are high because fishmeal includes ground bone. Vitamins are left out: the feed table lists none, and fishmeal vitamins vary with fish species and drying heat.

source.title: USDA FoodData Central — SR Legacy 173578: Fish oil, sardine
source.note: Fishmeal — GUESS for omega-3. Neither USDA nor the feed table gives fishmeal's fatty acids, so they are estimated as this entry's fat (10%) times the omega-3 share of USDA sardine oil (FDC 173578, a pelagic fish oil like anchoveta), assuming the fat left in fishmeal is like the oil pressed out of it. Sardine oil per 100 g: EPA + DHA 20.79 g, ALA 1.33 g. Fishmeal per gram: EPA + DHA 20.8 mg, ALA 0.0013 g. Fat in fishmeal oxidises during drying and storage, so the real figure may be lower.

source.title: USDA FoodData Central — SR Legacy 174182: Fish, anchovy, european, raw
source.note: Fishmeal — GUESS for vitamins. Neither USDA nor the feed table gives fishmeal vitamins, so they are scaled up from raw European anchovy (a close relative of the Peruvian anchoveta fishmeal is made from): B12, B6 and folate by protein (65 ÷ 20.35 g = 3.19×), vitamins A, E and K by fat (10 ÷ 4.84 g = 2.07×), vitamin C as anchovy's reported value. Per 100 g: vitamin b12 1.98 µg, vitamin b6 0.4568 mg, folate 28.75 µg DFE, vitamin a 30.99 µg RAE, vitamin e 1.178 mg, vitamin k 0.2066 µg, vitamin c 0 mg; divided by 100 for per-gram values. Fishmeal is cooked and dried at high heat, which destroys part of the B6, folate and vitamin A, so these are likely too high. Vitamin D is left out because USDA's raw anchovy doesn't report it. Only fills values missing from the main entries.

source.title: FAO (2014) — Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sectors
source.note: Fishmeal — yield_fraction: Set to 1.0 because fishmeal is used as-is in feed formulations with no further edible-fraction processing step; the entire product is the functional feed ingredient.

source.title: FAO (2014) — Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sectors
source.note: Fishmeal — emissions_per_kg: FAO fleet-level emission intensities for small pelagic capture fisheries (anchovy, sardine, herring) average 0.9–1.2 kg CO2e/kg landed fish for purse-seine operations. At a FIFO conversion of ~4.5 kg wet fish per kg fishmeal, vessel fuel emissions alone reach 4.0–5.4 kg CO2e/kg fishmeal. Adding fishmeal plant drying and processing energy (~0.5–1.0 kg CO2e/kg) gives a total range of 5–7 kg CO2e/kg. Central estimate 6.0 kg CO2e/kg used as a production-weighted midpoint across major fishmeal-producing nations (Peru, Chile, Denmark, Norway). CORRECTION 2026-09-24: the derivation is ~10-20x too high. Its premise that small-pelagic purse-seine fisheries emit 0.9–1.2 kg CO2e/kg landed conflicts with fishery LCAs: Peruvian anchoveta (the largest fishmeal fishery) emits 0.088–0.109 kg CO2e/kg landed and Peruvian fishmeal ~0.32 kg CO2e/kg meal cradle-to-export (Deville et al. 2025, source 277). The 4.5:1 fish-to-meal ratio is fine; the fuel intensity is not. Confidence lowered 3 -> 1.

source.title: Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) — Feeding Farmed Salmon: Is Organic Better? (Aquaculture)
source.note: Fishmeal — emissions_per_kg: Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) LCA of Norwegian Atlantic salmon feeds reports cradle-to-feed-mill emissions for conventional fishmeal at 5.0–8.0 kg CO2e/kg, central estimate ~6.5 kg CO2e/kg. Variability driven by source fishery fuel efficiency, drying technology (steam vs. direct-fire), and geographic origin. Consistent with the FAO fleet-level estimate (source 74) of 6.0 kg CO2e/kg. CORRECTION 2026-09-24: could not be verified: the URL's ScienceDirect pii (S0044848607009829) does not match Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) 'Feeding farmed salmon: Is organic better?' (Aquaculture 272:399–416, pii S0044848607005169), and a 5–8 kg CO2e/kg fishmeal range is an order of magnitude above recent fishmeal LCAs (~0.3 kg CO2e/kg, source 277). Confidence lowered 3 -> 1.

source.title: Deville et al. (2025) — Identifying current trends in the environmental impacts linked to fishmeal and fish oil production in Peru (Aquaculture 600:742239)
source.note: Fishmeal — farm_gate_emissions_per_kg: Deville et al. 2025 LCA of a Peruvian producer (~10% of national output; 169 anchoveta vessels, 4 plants, 2019 and 2021): ~320 kg CO2e per t fishmeal, energy allocation between meal and oil. Stages included: fishing (fuel ~45% of the total), reduction (cooking, pressing, drying — the processing step, included because animals eat the processed meal) and export transport. No land-use change applies. Existing emissions_per_kg is already cradle-to-feed-mill (no retail stages), but its magnitude is wrong — see correction. Confidence 2: single country (Peru is the largest producer and among the lowest-carbon); North-Atlantic fishmeal and plants on heavy fuel oil are higher, so the global mean is probably somewhat above 0.32. Added 2026-09-24 so animal feed is charged farm-gate, not retail, emissions.

source.title: Majluf, Matthews, Pauly, Skerritt & Palomares (2024) — A review of the global use of fishmeal and fish oil and the Fish In:Fish Out metric (Science Advances; PMC11482318)
source.note: Fishmeal — wild_fish_kg_per_kg: whole fish → 22.5% fishmeal + 5% fish oil by weight (industry averages); fish split between the two by mass, so each kg of meal or oil takes 1 ÷ 0.275 = 3.64 kg of fish. ~30% of fishmeal comes from trimmings of fish already caught for food, so only 70% is from fish killed for reduction: 3.64 × 0.70 = 2.55 kg whole wild fish per kg fishmeal.

source.title: Different ways of evolving tool-using brains in teleosts and amniotes (Communications Biology, 2024; PMC10786859)
source.note: Peruvian anchoveta (the main reduction fish) — neuron_count ESTIMATE using the same method as the other fish (source 384): 17.7 g body → 354.73 × (17.7/177.15)^0.5 = 112 mg brain → 1.669 × 112^0.706 = 46.7 M brain cells → ÷3 = 15.6 M neurons.

name: Fish Oil
notes:
Oil pressed from reduction fish (mostly anchoveta) during fishmeal production, fed mainly to farmed salmon. It's not eaten as food here.

Wild fish killed: each kg of meal or oil takes about 3.6 kg of fish. About half of fish oil comes from trimmings, so 1.78 kg of fish are killed per kg of fish oil.

Emissions are much higher per kg than fishmeal (~4.4 kg CO2e/kg in the Peruvian LCA), because fish yield little oil relative to meal. The split between meal and oil depends on the allocation method, which is why confidence is 2.

Vitamins and omega-3 come from a stand-in USDA record (sardine oil) because the feed source doesn't list them.

source.title: FAO (2014) — Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sectors
source.note: Fish oil — nutrition: Feed-grade fish oil is 100% lipid with no protein, fiber, or carbohydrate. Caloric density ~9.0 kcal/g (lipid energy standard). Saturated fat fraction approximately 27% of total fat for pelagic fish oil blends (anchovy/sardine/herring); EPA+DHA make up 25–35% of total fatty acids. Human nutritional database values are not applicable (feed ingredient); macros derived from standard fish oil product specifications in FAO aquaculture sector documentation.

source.title: USDA FoodData Central — SR Legacy 173578: Fish oil, sardine
source.note: Fish Oil — stand-in vitamins and omega-3: the FAO feed source has no vitamins, so they come from USDA's sardine oil, a pelagic fish oil like the anchovy/sardine/herring blends used in feed. Vitamins and minerals from USDA FDC 173578 per 100 g: vitamin a 0 µg RAE, vitamin c 0 mg, vitamin d 8.3 µg, folate 0 µg DFE, vitamin b12 0 µg, vitamin b6 0 mg, calcium 0 mg, iron 0 mg, magnesium 0 mg, potassium 0 mg, zinc 0 mg, phosphorus 0 mg, selenium 0 µg; not reported, so left out: vitamin e, vitamin k; divided by 100 for per-gram values. Omega-3 from FDC 173578 per 100 g: ALA 1.327 g (USDA's total 18:3, which is almost all ALA), EPA + DHA 20793 mg (EPA 10.137 + DHA 10.656); divided by 100 for per-gram values. Only fills values missing from the main entry.

source.title: FAO (2014) — Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sectors
source.note: Fish oil — yield_fraction: Set to 1.0 because fish oil is used as-is in feed formulations; the entire product is the functional feed ingredient.

source.title: FAO (2014) — Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sectors
source.note: Fish oil — emissions_per_kg: Fish oil is a co-product of fishmeal production at a yield ratio of roughly 1 kg oil per 5 kg fishmeal (by weight). Under economic allocation (oil valued at 2–3× fishmeal per kg due to omega-3 EFA content), fish oil receives approximately 35–55% of total upstream capture and processing emissions. Applying this allocation to the 5–7 kg CO2e/kg fishmeal footprint and scaling to oil yield gives ~2.5–4.0 kg CO2e/kg oil. Central estimate 3.5 kg CO2e/kg used, consistent with published aquaculture feed LCA studies using economic co-product allocation. CORRECTION 2026-09-24: the derivation scales an overstated fishmeal footprint (5–7 kg CO2e/kg; see fishmeal correction) and its source-74 text mixes mass and economic allocation shares. The 3.5 result happens to be near a direct LCA value (Peru, 4.43 kg CO2e/kg oil under energy allocation; source 277) but is not independently supported. Confidence lowered 3 -> 2.

source.title: Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) — Feeding Farmed Salmon: Is Organic Better? (Aquaculture)
source.note: Fish oil — emissions_per_kg: Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) report fish oil at 3.0–5.0 kg CO2e/kg under economic allocation (central estimate ~4.0 kg CO2e/kg) from the same cradle-to-feed-mill boundary used for fishmeal. Economic allocation is applied because fish oil commands a significant price premium over fishmeal per kg, driven by its omega-3 EFA (EPA/DHA) content which is the primary limiting nutrient in high-performance salmonid feeds. Corroborates the 3.5 kg CO2e/kg central estimate from source 74. CORRECTION 2026-09-24: the URL's ScienceDirect pii (S0044848607009829) does not match Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) (pii S0044848607005169), so the 3.0–5.0 range could not be checked. Confidence lowered 3 -> 2.

source.title: Deville et al. (2025) — Identifying current trends in the environmental impacts linked to fishmeal and fish oil production in Peru (Aquaculture 600:742239)
source.note: Fish oil — farm_gate_emissions_per_kg: Deville et al. 2025 Peruvian LCA: ~4,430 kg CO2e per t crude fish oil, energy allocation between fishmeal and oil. Stages included: fishing, reduction/oil separation, export transport. No land-use change. Confidence 2: single country, and the allocation choice drives the meal/oil split. Added 2026-09-24 so animal feed is charged farm-gate, not retail, emissions.

source.title: Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) — Feeding Farmed Salmon: Is Organic Better? (Aquaculture)

source.title: Majluf, Matthews, Pauly, Skerritt & Palomares (2024) — A review of the global use of fishmeal and fish oil and the Fish In:Fish Out metric (Science Advances; PMC11482318)
source.note: Fish oil — wild_fish_kg_per_kg: whole fish → 22.5% fishmeal + 5% fish oil by weight (industry averages); fish split between the two by mass, so each kg of meal or oil takes 1 ÷ 0.275 = 3.64 kg of fish. ~51% of fish oil comes from trimmings, so 49% is from fish killed for reduction: 3.64 × 0.49 = 1.78 kg whole wild fish per kg fish oil.

source.title: Different ways of evolving tool-using brains in teleosts and amniotes (Communications Biology, 2024; PMC10786859)
source.note: Peruvian anchoveta (the main reduction fish) — neuron_count ESTIMATE using the same method as the other fish (source 384): 17.7 g body → 354.73 × (17.7/177.15)^0.5 = 112 mg brain → 1.669 × 112^0.706 = 46.7 M brain cells → ÷3 = 15.6 M neurons.
